EXCEPTIONS TO THE PROPOSAL FOR DECISION BY JOHN GRIFFIN YATES, JR.
    WITH PROPOSED FINDINGS OF FACT AND CONCLUSIONS OF LAW

TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES:

         Intervenor John Griffin Yates, Jr. (“Yates”) files these Exceptions to the Proposal for

Decision (“PFD”), issued August 20, 2026, with Proposed Findings of Fact and Conclusions of

Law. These Exceptions track the organization of the PFD and address only the sections Yates

supports or challenges; sections needing no comment are omitted.1

    I.   INTRODUCTION
         Yates supports the ALJs’ recommendation to deny the applications of Oncor Electric

Delivery Company LLC and LCRA Transmission Services Corporation (“Applicants”) for the

proposed Bell County East-to-Big Hill and Big Hill-to-Sand Lake Projects.2 The ALJs correctly

found that Applicants did not prove the Projects are necessary for the service, accommodation,

convenience, or safety of the public under PURA § 37.056. 3 They also correctly found that

 Applicants’ failure to give the public-meeting notice required by 16 Texas Administrative Code

§22.52(a)(4) deprived roughly 1,400 landowners of due process, leaving denial as the only

meaningful remedy.4 Yates urges the Commission to adopt those recommendations.

          Yates files these Exceptions to reinforce those grounds for denial and to except to two parts

of the PFD: (1) the ALJs’ alternative recommendation of Route 894 should the Commission

approve any route;5 and (2) their conclusion that no analysis of the Projects’ cost to consumers

was required.6 If the Commission approves any route over Yates’s objections, it should choose

Route 296 or Route 392, or alternatively Route 487, and reject Route 894.

    II.   PROCEDURAL HISTORY
          Yates supports the ALJs’ decision in SOAH Order No. 12 to consolidate the issue of need

across Docket Nos. 59182 and 59475. 7 PURA § 37.0541 requires consolidation when the

applications or a motion to intervene show that the transmission lines in the separate proceedings

share a common point of interconnection. Consolidating the shared question of need was correct

and allowed a comprehensive determination of whether the Projects are necessary.

III.      APPLICABLE LAW
          Yates supports the ALJs’ statement of the governing law. The Commission may grant a

certificate only if it finds the facility necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience, or

safety of the public.8 In weighing a proposed line, the Commission must consider many factors—

some inherently in conflict with each other—and neither PURA nor the Commission’s rules fix

IV.     PRELIMINARY ORDER ISSUES 1-4

     A. Notice (Issues 2–3)
        Yates supports the ALJs’ findings that Applicants failed to satisfy the notice requirements

of Rule 22.52(a)(3) and Rule 22.52(a)(4).

        1. Notice of the Application
        Applicants failed to comply with Rule 22.52(a)(3)’s requirement of mailed notice to

directly affected landowners. The rule requires notice to the owners identified on the county tax

rolls on the date the application was filed—here, March 26, 2026.11 Applicants did not use the

current rolls as of that date. Applicants began compiling information from central appraisal district

records on December 8, 2025. As a result, more than three dozen directly affected landowners did

not receive timely notice of the Application.12

        2. Notice of Public Meeting
        The ALJs also correctly found that Applicants violated Rule 22.52(a)(4)’s public-meeting

notice requirement.13 After the June 2025 public meetings, Applicants expanded the study area by

roughly 400 miles of new route links, adding about 1,400 landowners to the class entitled to direct

mailed notice of the Application.14 Applicants mailed 2,809 invitations for the June 2025 meetings

but sent the March 26, 2026 application notices to more than 4,200 parties. 15 None of the

landowners affected by the later-added routes were ever invited to a public meeting to comment

before routing decisions are made, while application notice only tells landowners that a route

network has already been selected and a contested case has begun. 17 The two are not

interchangeable.

          Applicants are wrong to suggest the rule required only a public meeting keyed to the link

segments as they existed when that meeting was held.18 After the meetings, Applicants added

hundreds of miles of new links and brought roughly 1,400 more landowners within the class

entitled to application notice.19 When 25 or more landowners are affected, the rule entitles them to

the community-input process, and these landowners cannot be shut out of it.20 Applicants control

when they file an Application, and could have held another public meeting to comply with the

Rule.21 Because that process can no longer be provided in a way that cures the resulting prejudice,

denial is the only meaningful remedy.22 Yates supports that conclusion.

          Moreover, many directly affected landowners who would be able to attend a public meeting

would find the merits hearing inaccessible. The public meetings were held on weekday evenings

in three counties, close to affected landowners. The merits hearing was in Austin, during typical

business hours. To participate in the merits hearing, whether in person, or by Zoom, a landowner

had to be available Monday through Friday, between 9:00 a.m. and 5:00 p.m. Many landowners

could attend only by missing work or hiring counsel—a luxury that not everyone has. The merits

hearing was no substitute for the notice the rule requires.

          As the ALJs noted, the Texas Supreme Court has held that an executive-branch agency like

SOAH cannot resolve constitutional challenges.23 Yates therefore does not ask the Commission to

decide a due-process claim. Instead, below is a summary of the procedural concerns that further

reinforce the case for denial.

     A. The Measures, In Sequence
        This was a proceeding of extraordinary scale run on a severely compressed schedule.

Applicants filed the Application on March 26, 2026; the intervention deadline was April 27, 2026;

and the merits hearing began the second week of June 2026. The record grew to 823 testimonies,

1,398 exhibits, and hundreds of designated witnesses, and Applicants were still producing

discovery during the five-day hearing, forcing cross-examinations to be rescheduled. 24 Some

intervenors had only about three weeks to absorb this massive project before their deadline to

intervene.25 Even Staff’s witness, John Poole, had not read all the direct testimony when he filed

his own or when he was deposed.26

         The imbalance in public input was just as stark. The roughly 1,400 landowners added after

the June 2025 meetings had the least site-specific information and the least chance to shape routing

or contest need before the Application was filed.27 By the time they entered the case, the major

routing decisions had already been made without them.

         In short, an enormous case—involving vast amounts of data, filings, exhibits, witnesses,

affected landowners, and cost to the parties and to Texas ratepayers—was rushed at every stage.

That serves no one. It deprives almost everyone, except perhaps Applicants, of a fair opportunity

to participate meaningfully.

        B. How the Measures Accumulated
          The burdens of the compressed schedule were not separate; they compounded.28 As the

ALJs observed, landowners faced a near-immediate intervention deadline, entered a process in

which post-meeting route additions had already fixed much of the routing without their input, had

little time to cross-examine witnesses, and then had a single week to brief a record of more than

6,300 filings.29

VI.         NEED (ISSUES 5-7)
            The Commission may grant a CCN only on a showing that the proposed transmission

facility is necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public. 30

Applicants attempted to satisfy this burden through the testimony of Jared Gurley.31 Yates urges

the Commission to adopt the ALJs’ conclusion that Applicants failed to prove need.32

       A. HB 5066 Does Not Establish Need

            Through HB 5066, the Legislature instructed the Commission to direct ERCOT to develop

a reliability plan for the Permian Basin. Including a project in a reliability plan is not automatically

a finding that the project is needed. The Commission never approved the Permian Basin Reliability

Plan (“PBRP”) in a contested case, and need has not been predetermined.33

       B. The Forecasted Need Does Not Exist and Neither Does the Required Supply
          PURA § 37.056(c-1) directs the Commission to consider forecasted load growth, not

simply accept Applicants’ numbers. 34 Because officer-letter and data-center predictions had

proven overstated, ERCOT revised its forecasting methodology for non-oil-and-gas demand, and

         The projected oil-and-gas load fares no better. It rests on a single 2022 S&P Global study

that ERCOT never independently validated, built on the premise—since disproven—that oil-and-

gas producers had to electrify immediately to cut their greenhouse-gas profiles, leaving its

forecasts overstated and outdated.39

         For these reasons, ERCOT’s recommendation is not entitled to great weight. Under Rule

25.101(b)(3)(A)(ii), an ERCOT recommendation earns great weight only when quantifiable

evidence substantiates the projected load growth. 40 Here it does not, for two reasons: the

recommendation relies on a non-oil-and-gas forecast that ERCOT’s own realization-rate

methodology would sharply reduce,41 and it rests on the 2022 S&P Global study ERCOT never

verified.42

         Import Path 2 is offered as a reliability project, and its stated function depends on enough

generation being available to move power west to the Permian Basin.43 But when asked to identify

the central-or eastern-Texas generation available to serve Permian Basin load when power must

flow west, Applicants had no answer (the PBRP does not say, and Applicants have not analyzed

         Applicants never performed a partial-build study to justify Import Path 2 on its own. They

relied on the PBRP to assert that all three import paths are necessary—but that is not their burden,

and their own witness, Jared Gurley, admitted no study isolated Import Path 2.49 Applicants failed

         Finally, changed circumstances since the 2024 PBRP further undermine any need for

the Permian Basin, West Texas, and Panhandle/Northwest—approximately 39.467 GW of new

capacity—being developed at a scale that, as the ALJs found, rivals or exceeds the PBRP’s

projected load and could reduce or eliminate the need for Import Path 2.51 That in-basin generation

can serve Permian Basin load directly, yet Applicants did not account for it in claiming the line is

necessary.52

 VII.    ROUTING CRITERIA (ISSUES 8-10)
        Yates excepts to the ALJs’ alternative recommendation that, “should a route be selected

for construction, the ALJs recommend selection of Route 894.”53 If the Commission approves any

route, despite the failures of proof on need and the notice violations, it should select Route 296 or

Route 392—neither of which crosses Yates’s property—or, alternatively, Route 487, and it should

not select Route 894.

        The Commission must choose the route that best satisfies the statutory and regulatory

routing criteria.54 Among the four Focus Routes—296, 392, 487, and 894—the EA favors Routes

296 and 392 over Route 894 on the criteria the Commission weighs most heavily.55 Compared

with Route 894, which parallels existing transmission lines for only 5.66 miles, Routes 296 and

392 parallel far more—11.75 and 23.6 miles, respectively—and each runs alongside more existing

public roads.56 Route 296 also crosses less land of high historical-site potential than Route 894.57

Route 296’s total length parallel to existing compatible right-of-way also exceeds Route 894’s—

47.1% versus 43.9%.58 Routes 296 and 392 are also farther from Colorado Bend State Park and

Post Oak Ridge State Park,59 and Link J31 of Route 296 is the least worst option for crossing the

Colorado River.60 These are exactly the compatible-corridor and land-use considerations Rule

25.101(b)(3)(B) directs the Commission to weigh, and they favor Routes 296 and 392. Cost

provides no basis for preferring Route 894. On the EA’s own figures, Route 487 ($1.665 billion)

894 by only about $4 million—roughly one-quarter of one percent of the Project’s cost.61

         The ALJs’ main reservation about Route 296—that its centerline runs within 500 feet of

Florence Elementary School and two churches 62—does not outweigh its advantages or justify

Route 894 instead. No single factor is dispositive; the Commission must weigh them all together.63

Proximity to a school or church is a localized concern the Commission can address through

standard mitigation and, if needed, a minor centerline shift. Route 894, by contrast, uses Links J27

and J4 to permanently bisect an operating ranch. And any concern about Route 296’s proximity to

the school and churches is answered by Route 392, which raises no school-proximity issue. If the

Commission is troubled by Route 296 on that ground, Route 392 remains a full-avoidance

alternative, superior to Route 894.

         Route 894, by contrast, would inflict serious and avoidable harm on Yates’s land. Yates

owns 3,231 acres near Cherokee in San Saba County, held in his family for generations and used

for cattle grazing and hunting under long-standing family leases.64 Route 894 uses Links J27 and

J4.65 Link J4 runs along much of the property’s Highway 16 frontage, while Link J27 would bisect

Yates’s land. 66 The result is a permanent corridor that disrupts ranch operations, grazing, and

hunting, and access across the property.67 The routes would also pass near the old homestead and

would interfere with Yates’s plans to eventually retire on his property and build a home.68 The

land also holds a natural spring and a creek, Buffalo Creek, environmentally sensitive features

          Applicants’ own filings show these harms are avoidable. Many filed routes, including

 Routes 296 and 392, miss Yates’s property entirely, and several are among the shortest—and thus

 potentially cheapest—in the Application.71 Those alternatives defeat any claim that Route 894’s

 use of Links J27 and J4 is necessary. If a crossing truly cannot be avoided, Route 487 is far less

 damaging than Route 894: it uses Links J12 and J13 instead of J27 and J4, does not split the ranch

 in two, and avoids the Highway 16 frontage and the area around the homestead and planned home.

          The ALJs’ concern about Route 487 do not justify a preference for Route 894 over Route

 487. The § 25.101(b)(3)(B) factors most implicated by Yates’s land—paralleling existing

 compatible right-of-way, avoiding bifurcation of an operating ranch, and limiting impacts to

 homes and the Highway 16 frontage—favor Route 487 over Route 894. Because no single factor

 controls,72 Route 487’s closer proximity to parkland must be weighed against Route 894’s severe,

 permanent harm to the Yates property, and that balance favors Route 487. Yates therefore excepts

 to the recommendation of Route 894 and asks the Commission to select Route 296 or Route 392,

 or alternatively Route 487.

VIII.     OTHER PRELIMINARY ORDER ISSUES: COST TO CONSUMERS (ISSUES 11-

           Yates supports the ALJs’ finding that the Projects are not necessary to meet state or federal

reliability standards (Issue 11).73 On Issues 12 and 13, Applicants submitted neither the estimated

cost of the facilities to consumers nor the estimated congestion-cost savings.74

          Yates excepts to the ALJs’ conclusion that “the analysis for the cost to consumers and

congestion cost savings was not required, and the record contains no evidence quantifying

either.” 75 The cost of the Projects to consumers is unknown, no one tried to quantify it, and

ratepayers would simply pay whatever the Projects cost. For an undertaking of this size, that is

untenable—especially since the PFD itself notes an economic assessment estimating that the

proposed 765-kV buildout would impose nearly $100 billion in lifetime costs on Texas

ratepayers. 76 Where Applicants seek a certificate and a guaranteed return, the absence of any

consumer-cost or congestion-savings analysis weighs against approval and should not be excused.

Accordingly, Yates asks the Commission to reject the ALJs’ conclusion that no cost analysis was

required and to decline to approve the Projects without an estimate of their cost to consumers and

the resulting congestion-cost savings—or, at a minimum, to condition any approval on Applicants’

submission of that analysis.

IX.       CONCLUSION

          For these reasons, Yates respectfully asks the ALJs to recommend, and the Commission to

enter, a final order that:


          A.         Denies the Applications because Applicants failed to prove that the Projects are

                                           APPENDIX A

                    Yates’s Proposed Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law

Proposed Findings of Fact

1. Applicants filed the Application on March 26, 2026; the deadline to intervene was April 27,

2026; and the hearing on the merits began the second week of June 2026.

2. After the June 2025 public meetings, Applicants expanded the study area by roughly 400 miles

of new route links, bringing approximately 1,400 additional landowners within the class entitled

to direct mailed notice of the Application.

3. Applicants mailed 2,809 invitations for the June 2025 public meetings but sent the March 26,

2026 application notices to more than 4,200 parties.

4. None of the landowners affected by the later-added routes was invited to a public meeting to

comment on those routes before the Application was filed.

5. Applicants did not provide mailed notice based on the county tax rolls current as of March 26,

2026.

6. In its 2025 RTP, ERCOT reduced its forecasted 2031 summer peak demand from 218 gigawatts

to 159 gigawatts.

7. The PBRP load forecast has not been retested against ERCOT’s adjusted methodology for

validating loads, and applying that methodology reduces the projected load by at least 3,571 MW.

8. Applicants performed no partial-build study isolating the need for Import Path 2, and

Applicants’ witness acknowledged the absence of such a study.

9. Applicants submitted neither the estimated cost of the proposed facilities to consumers nor the

estimated congestion-cost savings.




                                               18
 10. Route 894 would use Links J27 and J4 to bifurcate the Yates ranch and run along its Highway

16 frontage, while Routes 296 and 392 avoid the Yates property entirely and Route 487 crosses it

less severely.

Proposed Conclusions of Law

1. The Commission may grant a CCN amendment only if Applicants prove, by a preponderance

of the evidence, that the Projects are necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience, or

safety of the public. PURA § 37.056.

2. Applicants did not carry that burden, and the Projects are not necessary under PURA § 37.056.

3. Applicants failed to comply with the public-meeting notice requirement of 16 TAC §

22.52(a)(4), depriving approximately 1,400 landowners of the process due them.

4. Because the remedy prescribed by the rule can no longer cure the resulting prejudice, denial of

the Application is the appropriate remedy.

5. Should the Commission approve any route, the routing criteria of 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B)

favor Route 296 or Route 392, or in the alternative Route 487, over Route 894.
